metrics.gist: The most reported LinkedIn design question. Collect `[source, metric, value]` from hundreds of machines, store it as **time series**, let people **graph** any metric for any hosts over time, and **alert** on thresholds. The hard parts: very high **write volume**, fast **range queries**, and alerting that does not miss or spam.
clarify: How many sources and metrics, how often?
Decides write rate — the main number in this question.
How long to keep data, and at what detail?
Raw for days, then downsampled (1-min, 1-hour) — decides storage.
How fresh must graphs and alerts be?
Alerts within ~1 minute usually; graphs a few seconds behind is fine.
Which queries? One metric for a few hosts (t1→t2), or aggregates (p99 across a cluster)?
Decides the data layout and pre-aggregation.
Push or pull — can we put an agent on every machine?
Decides the collection path.
deep: Data layout
Group points by series (metric + source) and time block (e.g. 2 hours). A graph query reads a few contiguous blocks. Compress timestamps and values with deltas — this is why TSDBs are so small.
Downsampling
Nobody needs 10-second points from last year. Keep raw for ~2 weeks, 1-minute for months, 1-hour for years. The query service chooses the resolution from the range.
Alerting that works
"Above 70% for 5 minutes", not "above 70% once" (avoids flapping). Treat **missing data as a signal** — a dead host sends nothing. Group and dedupe alerts during incidents.
Cardinality
The real danger: a label like user_id creates millions of series and kills the TSDB. Limit labels, and reject or sample high-cardinality metrics.
followups: Write rate goes 10× — what breaks first?
The TSDB write path. Add shards by series, batch harder on agents, drop or sample low-value metrics. Kafka absorbs short spikes.
Graph a cluster-wide p99 over 30 days fast.
Pre-aggregate per cluster in rollups (or store histograms/sketches); never compute it from raw points at query time.
The monitoring system itself goes down.
Run it per data centre; each DC monitors itself and the others. Agents buffer locally. A separate tiny heartbeat checker watches the monitor.
Host health across 3 data centres (the InterviewDB version).
Per-DC collectors and storage, a global view that merges them, and a current-state store (latest status per host) for "what is unhealthy now".
How do you avoid alert spam?
For-duration conditions, grouping by service, dedupe, severity levels, silence windows during maintenance.
mistakes: Writing every point straight into a SQL table.
No downsampling — storage grows forever, week-long graphs are slow.
Alerting on a single sample (flapping).
Forgetting that a silent host is a failure.
Ignoring cardinality.
metrics.say: "Agents batch to Kafka, a sharded time-series store keeps compressed series with rollups, queries pick the resolution from the range, and alerts evaluate for-duration rules on the stream — with missing data treated as an alert."

kvstore.gist: Build a key-value store on top of a **simple file API** (create, append, read bytes at an offset). Keys fit in memory, values do not. This is the **Bitcask** design: append values to a log file, keep an **in-memory index key → (file, offset, size)**.
clarify: Exact interface given?
Yes — append, read at offset, create. So no in-place updates — everything is append.
Delete support?
Needs tombstones and compaction.
Durability on crash?
Need to rebuild the index from files.
Single machine or distributed?
Start with one node; distribution is a follow-up.
deep: Write path
Append to the end of the active file (fast, sequential), then update the index. An update is just a new append — the index points to the newest one.
Read path
Look up the key in memory, then read exactly `size` bytes at `offset`. One disk read.
Delete and compaction
Append a tombstone; index removes the key. Compaction later removes old values and tombstones to free space.
Crash recovery
Rebuild the index by scanning files (or hint files). A checksum per record detects a half-written last record — ignore it.
The distributed version (two of the three LeetCode reports)

Partition keys with **consistent hashing** (virtual nodes so adding a node moves little data). Replicate each partition to 3 nodes. Consistency: quorum reads/writes (W + R > N) for strong-ish reads, or leader-per-partition for simple strong consistency. Name the trade: availability during partitions vs fresh reads.
followups: Range queries (all keys between A and B)?
A hash index cannot do it — use a sorted structure (LSM tree / SSTables) instead. Say the trade-off.
Keys no longer fit in memory.
Move to an LSM tree: sorted files with a sparse index and Bloom filters.
Make it distributed.
Partition keys by consistent hashing; replicate each partition to 3 nodes.
Concurrent writers?
One writer thread appends (serialises writes); readers read in parallel.
Partitioning, replication and consistency — how?

Consistent hashing with virtual nodes; replication factor 3; leader-follower per partition (simple, strong) or leaderless quorum N=3, W=2, R=2 (more available). Hinted handoff and read repair for leaderless.
Disk cleanup — when do you run compaction, and does it hurt reads?
Compact when dead data in a file passes a threshold (e.g. 50%); run in the background with an I/O budget; readers keep using old files until the swap is atomic.
How do you know what is safe to delete after compaction?
Write the new file fully, fsync, update the index to point at it, then delete the old file. A crash in between leaves extra files, never lost data.
mistakes: Trying to update values in place — the API only appends.
Forgetting compaction — disk grows forever.
No checksum for torn writes after a crash.
kvstore.say: "Append-only data files, an in-memory index of key to file and offset, background compaction, and hint files for fast restart — the Bitcask design."

topn.gist: Find the **top N most frequent items over a fixed 24-hour window** across hundreds of machines. You cannot ship every request to one place, so each machine **counts locally**, and you **merge** counts. Exact vs approximate is the key trade-off.
clarify: Exact top N, or approximately right is fine?
Exact needs much more memory and network. Approximate allows Count-Min Sketch / Space-Saving.
"Last 24 hours (not any 24 hours)" — a fixed day or a sliding window?
The wording says a specific window — fixed hourly buckets make this easy.
How big is N? 10 or 10,000?
Small N → small heaps.
How fast must the answer be? Ad hoc query or a daily report?
Decides precompute vs on-demand merge.
deep: Why local top-K is approximate
An item that is #10,001 on every machine can still be #1 overall. Fix: send more than N (10× N) and add a second pass for exact counts of the candidates, or accept small error and say so.
Count-Min Sketch + heap
Fixed memory counts with small overestimate; a heap keeps current top-K. Good when keys are too many to store exactly.
Sliding vs fixed
Hourly buckets give a window accurate to one hour. Need minute accuracy → minute buckets (1,440 of them).
Several windows at once (5 min, 1 hour, 24 hours)
Keep minute buckets. 5 min = merge 5 buckets; 1 hour = 60; 24 hours = merge hourly rollups (each hour merged once and stored). Same pipeline, three cheap merges.
followups: Exact answer is required.
Two passes: first collect candidate keys from every machine's top-K, then ask every machine for exact counts of those candidates.
Query must return in milliseconds.
Keep a precomputed rolling result updated every hour (or minute).
One machine is down for an hour.
Its bucket is missing — mark the result as partial, backfill when it returns (agents buffer locally).
Different windows: last 1 hour, last 7 days.
Same hourly buckets — merge 1 or 168 of them.
Do you need a coordination service (ZooKeeper)?

No — a candidate lost points adding one. Machines just send counts to aggregators partitioned by key; nothing here needs leader election or locks. Only add a component when you can say exactly what breaks without it.
mistakes: Sending every request to a central counter.
Merging only top-N from each machine and calling it exact.
Not asking exact vs approximate.
topn.say: "Count locally in hourly buckets, ship each machine's top-K, merge 24 buckets for the answer — approximate by default, with a second exact pass if needed."

typeahead.gist: Suggestions while typing must come back in **under ~100 ms**. So you **precompute** the top suggestions for every prefix and serve them from memory. Personalisation (your connections first) and freshness (new names) are the follow-ups.
clarify: What do we suggest — people, companies, skills, all?
Different sources, mixed in one list.
Personalised (your network first) or the same for everyone?
LinkedIn: personalised matters a lot — "Ry" should show your connection Ryan.
How fresh? A new company must show within?
Minutes vs a day decides batch vs streaming updates.
Latency target?
Under 100 ms end to end, so the server part ~20–30 ms.
deep: Precompute top-K per prefix
Ranking millions of matches at query time is too slow. Store the answer for each prefix ahead of time. Space grows, but memory is cheap compared to latency.
Personalisation without per-user tries
Global index for popular entities + a small per-user list of connections, merged at query time.
Freshness
Main index rebuilt daily; a small "recent additions" index updated in near real time and merged in.
followups: How to scale with 1 billion users in the index?
Shard the prefix index by prefix; replicate hot shards (short prefixes like "a" are hottest); cache top prefixes.
How to generate rank and return top K with low latency?
Scores computed offline (popularity, connections, recency), stored sorted per prefix, so query time is just a lookup + small merge.
Typos ("Rian" for "Ryan")?
Fuzzy matching with edit distance 1 on short candidate sets, or phonetic keys.
Privacy?
Only show names the viewer is allowed to see; filter blocked members.
mistakes: Ranking at query time over the whole dataset.
Forgetting personalisation for LinkedIn.
No client-side debounce/cancel.
typeahead.say: "Precompute top-K per prefix in a sharded in-memory index, merge with a small personal list of connections at query time, and keep it fresh with a small real-time index."

denylist.gist: Detect bad IPs in one place and push the list to thousands of web servers **quickly and reliably**. The real problem is **distribution**: every server must get updates fast, and the check on every request must cost almost nothing.
clarify: How fast must a new bad IP be blocked everywhere?
Seconds vs minutes changes push vs pull.
How big is the list? IPv4 only or IPv6 too?
A few million IPs fit in memory on each server. IPv6 needs prefixes (ranges), not single IPs.
Do entries expire?
Yes usually — IPs get reused. Add a TTL so the list does not grow forever.
Is a false positive (blocking a good user) worse than missing a bad one?
Decides how strict detection is and whether we need an appeal / allow-list path.
deep: Push vs pull

Pull every 30 s is simple but slow and makes 10,000 servers hit the service at once. Push through Kafka is fast (seconds). Best: **push deltas, plus a periodic pull of the version** to catch anything missed.
Never stale without knowing it
Each server knows its list version. If it falls too far behind (version gap or no update for N minutes) it reloads the snapshot and raises an alert.
What if the denylist service is down?
Web servers keep using their last list — fail open for availability, but the list is still mostly correct. Never block all traffic because the list could not load.
Ranges and IPv6
Store CIDR prefixes in a trie (longest-prefix match). One entry can block a whole bad subnet.
"Intercept malicious requests" (the second LeetCode wording)

Where you intercept matters: at the edge (load balancer / API gateway) so bad traffic never reaches services. The in-memory denylist check runs there. isMaliciousRequest is expensive, so call it asynchronously on a sample or on suspicious traffic and feed results into the denylist, rather than calling it on every request.
followups: A bad IP must be blocked in under 5 seconds everywhere.
Push via Kafka with servers subscribed directly; measure end-to-end lag as a metric and alert on it.
The list becomes 100M entries.
Use a Bloom filter in memory for the first check (no false negatives), and confirm hits against a local compact store. Or block by prefix instead of single IPs.
How do you unblock a wrongly blocked user?
Allow-list that overrides the denylist, an appeal path, and TTLs so mistakes expire on their own.
How do you check it is working?
Metrics: list version per server, lag, block rate, false-positive reports. Canary: add a test IP and confirm every server blocks it.
Must isMaliciousRequest run on every request?
Usually no — too slow. Check the cheap in-memory denylist on every request, run the expensive classifier async (or only on suspicious patterns), and add offenders to the list.
mistakes: Calling a remote service on every request — adds latency and a single point of failure.
Sending the full list every time instead of deltas.
No versioning — you cannot tell which servers are stale.
Running isMalicious inline and slowing every request.
denylist.say: "Detect off the request path, keep a versioned source of truth, push deltas to an in-memory copy on every server, and let servers self-heal with snapshots when they fall behind."

mq.gist: Design a **Kafka-like** queue: producers append messages, consumers read them, messages are **durable** and **ordered within a partition**. LinkedIn built Kafka, so expect deep questions on partitions, replication and delivery guarantees.
clarify: Queue (each message to one consumer) or pub/sub (to many groups)?
Kafka style log does both via consumer groups.
Ordering needed?
Usually per key — so partition by key.
Delivery: at-least-once or exactly-once?
At-least-once + idempotent consumers is the common answer.
Retention — delete after read, or keep for days?
Log style keeps for days, so consumers can replay.
api: consume(topic, group) → messages from an offset
deep: Why an append-only log is fast
Sequential disk writes and reads, OS page cache, batching, zero-copy send. That is why Kafka handles huge throughput.
Replication and acks
Leader writes, followers copy. With acks=all, a message is acknowledged only when all in-sync replicas have it — no loss if the leader dies.
Delivery guarantees
Consumer processes then commits the offset → at-least-once (may repeat after a crash). Make consumers idempotent. Exactly-once needs transactions — say it is costly.
followups: A consumer is slow (lag grows).
Add consumers up to the number of partitions; more partitions for the future; alert on lag.
A broker dies.
Controller elects a new leader from in-sync replicas; producers and consumers refresh metadata.
Ordering across the whole topic?
Only with one partition — kills throughput. Per-key ordering is the usual answer.
Delayed / scheduled messages?
Separate delay topics or a timer service — Kafka does not do it natively.
mistakes: A single queue with no partitions.
Promising global ordering and high throughput together.
Deleting messages on read (no replay).
mq.say: "Partitioned, replicated append-only logs; producers partition by key for order; consumer groups track offsets for at-least-once delivery with idempotent consumers."

notify.gist: One pipeline that takes "something happened" events and delivers notifications over **push, email and in-app**, respecting **user preferences**, **deduplication**, **rate limits** and **retries**. The key is to separate deciding *what* to send from actually *sending*.
clarify: Which events? Messages, likes, job alerts, security?
Priority differs — security codes must be fast, digests can wait.
User preferences per channel and type?
Needs a preference service checked on every send.
Volume?
Decides queues and worker counts.
Digests (batch many likes into one)?
Needs a delay/aggregation step.
deep: Priority queues
A security code should not wait behind 1M marketing emails — separate high-priority queues and workers.
Idempotency
Each notification has an id; workers check before sending so a retry does not send twice.
Rate limiting the user
Cap notifications per user per hour; collapse many "X liked your post" into one.
Per-category limits ("5 marketing notifications per day per user")

Counter per (user, category, day) in Redis with expiry — atomic increment, reject or delay when over. Transactional and security categories are never limited. Check limits **after** preferences and **before** sending.
followups: A provider (APNs) is slow or down.
Queue grows; retry with backoff; circuit breaker; fall back to in-app.
Track delivery and opens.
Delivery receipts from providers + open/click events back into analytics.
Send at a good local time.
Schedule non-urgent notifications for the user's daytime.
Too many notifications annoy users.
Per-user budget and ranking — send only the most valuable ones.
Add rate limits per category.
Per (user, category, day) counters; different limits per category; over the limit → drop or merge into a digest. Never limit security codes.
Where do user preferences sit?
A preference service checked first (opt-outs per channel and category, quiet hours); cached because it is read on every notification.
mistakes: Services calling email/push providers directly.
One queue for everything.
No dedupe on retries.
Ignoring preferences.
notify.say: "Events go to a notification service that applies preferences, dedupe, rate limits and digests, then to per-channel priority queues whose workers retry idempotently."

scheduler.gist: Run jobs at the right time on machines you **ask for through an API**, make sure each job runs **once**, survive scheduler crashes, and **alert** on failures. The core: a durable job store, a way to find **due jobs** quickly, **leases** so two schedulers never run the same job, and a clear **job state machine**.
clarify: One-off jobs, recurring (cron), or both? Dependencies between jobs?
Recurring needs a "next run time"; dependencies need a DAG — say if out of scope.
Exactly once, or at least once with idempotent jobs?
Exactly once is very hard; at-least-once + idempotent jobs is the usual answer.
What does the machine API give us — a free machine on request? Can machines die mid-job?
Decides retries and heartbeats.
How many jobs per day, and how late is acceptable?
Decides how we find due jobs (DB index vs time buckets).
Alert on what — failure, timeout, too many retries, late start?
Defines the alerting rules.
api: POST /jobs {cron or runAt, command, resources, retries, timeout}
deep: No double runs

A scheduler **claims** a run with an atomic update: `SET state=claimed, lease_until=now+30s WHERE id=? AND state=due`. Only one wins. If it crashes, the lease expires and another scheduler picks it up.
State machine
scheduled → claimed → running → succeeded / failed → (retry → scheduled) / dead. Every change is an atomic update with the expected old state, so late messages cannot move a run backwards.
Machine failure mid-job

Workers heartbeat every few seconds. Missed heartbeats → the monitor marks the run lost and schedules a retry (with backoff), on a new machine from the API. Jobs must be idempotent because a retry may repeat work.
Top-of-hour spike
Partition due runs by hash across scheduler nodes; add small random jitter for jobs that do not need the exact second.
followups: Do you need ZooKeeper / a coordination service?
Not for claiming runs — an atomic DB update with a lease is enough. Use one only if you need leader election for something singular. (A candidate lost points for adding one that was not needed.)
The machine API is slow or has no free machines.
Queue the run as waiting-for-capacity, retry with backoff, alert if it starts too late.
Jobs depend on other jobs.
Store a DAG; a run becomes due when its parents succeed.
Exactly-once execution?
Not guaranteed across crashes — make jobs idempotent (unique run id, check before side effects).
How do users see what happened?
Run history with logs link, status, attempts; dashboards on success rate and lateness.
mistakes: Two schedulers can pick the same job (no atomic claim).
No heartbeats — a dead machine leaves a job "running" forever.
Scanning the whole job table every second.
Promising exactly-once.
Adding a coordination service you cannot justify.
scheduler.say: "Durable job store with a due-time index, atomic lease-based claims so a run executes once at a time, heartbeats and timeouts drive retries on new machines from the API, and every terminal failure raises an alert."

ratelimit.gist: Limit how many requests a client can make per time window. Know the algorithms (**token bucket**, sliding window), and the **distributed** problem: many servers must share the count without adding much latency.
clarify: Limit by what — user, IP, API key, endpoint?
Decides the counter key.
Hard limit or small overshoot OK?
Exact needs a shared store; approximate allows local counters.
Burst allowed?
Token bucket allows bursts; fixed window does not shape them.
Where — API gateway or inside each service?
Usually at the gateway.
api: HTTP 429 with Retry-After header when over
deep: Algorithms

Fixed window: simple, but allows 2× bursts at window edges. Sliding window log: exact but stores every timestamp. Sliding window counter: good approximation. **Token bucket**: refill rate + bucket size, allows controlled bursts — the common choice.
Atomic update
Read-check-write must be atomic, or two gateways both let the last request through. Use a Redis Lua script.
Failure mode
If Redis is down: fail open (allow) for normal APIs, fail closed for expensive or security-sensitive ones. Say which.
followups: Make it fast — no Redis call per request.
Local token buckets per gateway with a share of the limit; sync every second. Small overshoot accepted.
Different limits per customer plan.
Rules service with per-plan config, cached locally.
Multi-region.
Per-region limits, or route a key to a home region.
Protect against one hot key.
Local pre-check before Redis; reject obvious abusers at the edge.
mistakes: Non-atomic check-then-increment.
Not saying what happens when the counter store is down.
Only knowing fixed windows.
ratelimit.say: "Token bucket per key at the gateway, state in Redis updated atomically by a Lua script, with a stated fail-open or fail-closed policy and a local-counter option for lower latency."

logging.gist: Collect logs from many services, move them reliably, store them cheaply, and make them **searchable** and usable for **analytics**. Separate the **ingest path** (fast, buffered) from **storage/query** (indexed hot data, cheap cold data).
clarify: What queries — search by text, or aggregate analytics (counts by field)?
Search needs an index (Elasticsearch); analytics needs columnar storage.
Volume?
Decides partitions and cost.
Retention?
Hot 7 days searchable, cold 1 year in object storage is common.
Can we lose logs?
Usually small loss OK for debug logs, not OK for audit logs.
api: Analytics: SQL over the log tables
deep: Back-pressure
If storage is slow, Kafka buffers; agents buffer on disk. Logging must never crash or slow the service — drop debug logs first if needed.
Structured logs
JSON with fields (time, service, level, traceId) makes both search and analytics easy.
Cost control
Sampling, shorter retention for debug level, compression, tiered storage.
followups: Find all logs for one request across services.
Add a trace id to every log line and index it.
Ingest spikes 10×.
Kafka absorbs it; scale processors; sample low-priority logs.
Audit logs must never be lost.
Separate pipeline with acks=all, replication, no sampling.
Real-time alerts from logs.
A stream consumer counting error patterns and alerting.
mistakes: Services writing directly to the search cluster.
Keeping everything in the expensive index forever.
Unstructured text logs.
logging.say: "Agents ship to Kafka, processors parse and enrich, recent logs go to a search index and everything goes to cheap columnar storage, with buffering so logging never hurts the service."
